results.title: Common Desktop Support Issues and Solutions | M7
results.content:
## Computer Won’t Start

A computer that won’t boot up is one of the most frustrating desktop support issues. There are several potential reasons for this, ranging from power supply failures to system corruption.

### Causes

 Power supply failure
 Hardware failure (e.g., motherboard, hard drive)
 Corrupted operating system files
 Loose or disconnected cables
 BIOS issues

### Solutions [...] ### Solutions

 Check System Requirements: Ensure that the software is compatible with the version of the operating system running on the computer.
 Run Compatibility Mode: In some cases, running older software in compatibility mode can resolve issues. Right-click the program, select Properties, and choose a previous version of Windows to run it under.
 Install Updates: Ensure that both the operating system and the software in question are up to date.
 Contact Software Vendor: If the software is still malfunctioning, contacting the software vendor for a patch or solution may be necessary.

## Solve Your Most Frustrating Desktop Support Issues With M7 Services [...] ## Different Types of Desktop Support Issues and Solutions

Understanding how to troubleshoot and resolve the following common desktop support problems can significantly reduce downtime and improve productivity:

## Slow Computer Performance

One of the most common complaints users have is that their computer is running slowly. This issue can stem from several factors, including overloaded system resources, software conflicts, or even hardware issues.

 Too many programs running at once
 Malware or viruses consuming system resources
 Insufficient RAM or hard drive space
 Outdated drivers or software
 Fragmented hard drive

results.title: Everything's broken and nobody's upset - Scott Hanselman's Blog
results.content:
So, your amazing feat of engineering phone, with color retina display, video capabillity, 700,000 apps etc has some extra stuff taking drive space (of the 16GB device).  
  
Your amazing, multi million line Windows desktop, the work of some 1000 people or more, has a problem with indexing.  
  
The network and apps that connects you via email to everyone else on the planet, free, globally and instantly, sometimes loses a mail. Or is slow to load your new messages.  
  
A program with which you can do what it took huge teams, million dollars of equipment, and professional expertise to do (FCP), has a crashing bug in some particular action.  
  
The program that lets you talk to everybody on the planet, instantly, with video, and paying nothing, has a badly designed UI.  
  
etc... [...] I do remember one head-scratcher a few years ago with OS X, where the home user folder would just keep growing over time even if the user didn't save anything. It was enough years ago that it became a problem if something was taking up an extra 2GB on a desktop machine. It turned out the culprit was Mail.app, and the way it indexed emails; I don't know about today, but a few years ago they used SQLite. It's a nice library--for those who don't know, it 's a SQL implementation meant to be used as a library, and saves databases to a file--but Apple's index files would just grow no matter what. There were a slew of shareware apps that solved the problem of growing index files, of various prices, and they all did the same thing: they opened the indexes and ran "VACUUM DEFS;" [...] etc...  
  
Yes, I can see how "everything is broken".  
  
Because when you didn't have any of these, when 30 years before you had a rotating dial to dial numbers on your phone,   
20 years before 20MB was a huge disk in a desktop system, and 10 years before something like video chat was only possible  
in huge organizations with special software, everything was perfect...

results.content:
[]( Center

# Browser Troubleshooting

If you have trouble with the Capacity Admin Console, you may be experiencing an issue with your internet browser. Common browser issues include:

 Trouble receiving a Admin link
 Not receiving an answer from the Capacity Bot
 Slow or delayed answers from the Capacity Bot

### Browser Troubleshooting Tips

For browser issues, try the following troubleshooting tips: [...] Make sure that your browser is up-to-date. Here are instructions on how to find out if you’re running the latest versions of our supported desktop browsers: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer 11.
 Clear the cache on your browser. Instructions for clearing your cache will vary depending on your browser. Accessing the Help menu on your browser should allow you to locate step-by-step instructions.
 Switch to a different browser: Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox or IE11. Again, double check that you are running the most up-to-date version of these browsers.

### Enable Cookies [...] ### Enable Cookies

Signing into Capacity’s Admin Console page requires that your browser has cookies enabled. To make sure cookies are enabled in your browser, click the link below that corresponds to your browser type, and follow the instructions listed on the page to enable cookies.

 Google Chrome
 Firefox
 Safari
 Edge
 Internet Explorer 11

Once this is done, navigate back to the Capacity Admin Console, enter your account email on the login page, and try signing in again.

If none of the above tips resolve your issue, please get in touch with our support team at support@capacity.com.

results.title: How Do You Deal With "My Computer Is Slow, I Need a New One" Complaints? - IT & Tech Careers - Spiceworks Community
results.content:
The Execs are the worst offenders. It’s an uphill battle.

We have Execs like this. Mostly we let THEM pick their equipment - within reason (only from OUR vendors, only OUR OSs, etc.) Then they have a harder time complaining about the speed since they did the capacity planning. Obviously this only works with certain types of budgeting processes.

One way I have come across to alleviate this “slow” issue is a two fold solution. [...] # How Do You Deal With "My Computer Is Slow, I Need a New One" Complaints?

This problem user is a VP (why, I don’t have a clue). She specializes in throwing people under the proverbial bus. A couple of months ago, we gave her a brand new Dell Laptop with a docking station. The laptop is faster than all IT desktops–Intel Core 2 with 4 GB of RAM.

This user has had issues with her computer for months. Each time she exaggerates the issue. Today she calls me bitching about her computer being “slow”. “Slow” is a vague and broad description of a problem. All I can do is hypothesize. She doesn’t like this. So I have her log in while I shadow her remotely. The computer was fine. Supposedly the issue only happens when she’s using Outlook. The computer freezes up and she has to hard boot it. [...] 2.When you have been round to their desk and still not seen any issues, after doing some useless stuff like looking in MSConfig, Ping testing the the servers, flushing DNS cache, checking installed programs etc,. What you need to say is “The fault doesn’t seem to be occurring at the moment, unfortunately this makes it impossible to diagnose and fix. What we need to do is have me either remote in or come round the next time it happens. So give me a call the next time it runs slow and I can see the problem first hand.” This again says you do care that there is a fault and that you can fix it but not until you see it.

results.title: The Best PCs (Desktop Computers) We've Tested for 2026 | PCMag
results.content:
While a desktop's SSD stores your data, its system memory (or RAM) works in conjunction with the CPU to run applications and helps define its capacity to multitask. Memory capacities of 8GB or 16GB are fine for most users, and these are the most common configurations on entry-level or midrange desktops of all forms and sizes.

Few of you will see much benefit from memory amounts above 16GB, but you'll find exceptions. Quality gaming PCs should have at least 16GB of RAM, and 32GB is a prudent upgrade if you're an esports enthusiast who wants to play and stream in-game footage simultaneously.
